analysis: Examined the two base_text units of fixtures/prompt-contract/v1/production_vectors.json (base lines 3778-5074). They contain only synthetic public cache-parity vectors: repeated 'Public synthetic cache-parity input', token ID arrays, chain hashes, prompt_contract_id and block boundaries. No secrets, credentials, keys, or real consumer data (A-001) are visible. The patch excerpt and file_changes show the change is a test-fixture regeneration: it adds additional_context {enable_thinking:false} to template inputs, shifts prompt_token_count (803->767) and block boundaries (the 768 block is dropped), and updates chain hashes and token IDs. This is a data-only fixture with no executable code, authorization, attestation (TB-011, TB-002), encryption, or billing logic changed. The security-relevant concern is indirect: these vectors pin prompt-contract and prefix-cache chain hashes (T-041, TB-007). If the Swift provider and coordinator/platform implementations consume the same fixture, a mismatch could cause cache-key divergence. That would be a correctness or availability issue, not a confidentiality regression visible here. Head-side text was not supplied, only base text and a truncated patch, so I could not verify that the new hashes and tokens are internally consistent or that the template change (enable_thinking) is applied consistently on the producer and consumer sides. The cache-key domain separation, per-scope isolation (scope_id 'fixture-scope') and tenant-scoping logic are not in this diff. No regression is identified; the remaining integration question is whether the corresponding code changes (not in this batch) preserve the cache-key and prompt-contract binding for T-041.
